```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2,
                      dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

Computer-based tests record how long each response took. mirtverse uses those times
together with a fitted mirt model, following van der Linden's (2007) hierarchical
framework:

* **Time intensity** ($\beta_j$): how long item *j* takes on average (log scale).
* **Time discrimination** ($\alpha_j$): how consistently the item's times reflect a
  person's speed.
* **Speed** ($\tau_i$): how fast person *i* works, correlated with ability $\theta_i$.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(mirtverse)
```

## Simulated example

`sim_rt()` generates responses and response times; here 8% of examinees rapid-guess
on some items.

```{r}
sim <- sim_rt(N = 1500, J = 20, rho = -0.3, rapid = 0.08, seed = 2026)
mod <- mirt(sim$responses, 1, verbose = FALSE)
fit <- fit_rt(mod, sim$rt)
fit
```

```{r}
interpret(fit)
```

## Rapid guessing

Two rules are available. The default `"residual"` rule flags a response that is much
faster than expected for that person on that item. The `"nt10"` rule flags responses
faster than 10% of the item's mean time (Wise & Ma, 2012).

```{r}
mean(fit$flags[sim$rapid])   # share of simulated rapid guesses detected
mean(fit$flags[!sim$rapid])  # false alarms
```

```{r}
autoplot(fit, "rapid")
autoplot(fit, "rte")
```

Response time effort (RTE) is each examinee's share of non-rapid responses
(Wise & Kong, 2005). Examinees below .90 are often excluded before reporting
group results (motivation filtering).

```{r}
persons <- augment(fit)
head(persons)
```

## Item parameters and the ability-speed relation

```{r}
tidy(fit)
autoplot(fit, "items")
autoplot(fit, "persons")
```

## Notes

The item response parameters are taken from the mirt model and held fixed; the
response-time parameters, speed variance and ability-speed correlation are estimated
by marginal maximum likelihood. Because times act as collateral information, the
joint ability estimates (`theta`) can be slightly more precise than the
response-only estimates (`theta_responses_only`) when ability and speed are strongly
correlated.

## References

van der Linden, W. J. (2007). A hierarchical framework for modeling speed and accuracy
on test items. *Psychometrika, 72*, 287-308.

Wise, S. L., & Kong, X. (2005). Response time effort: A new measure of examinee
motivation in computer-based tests. *Applied Measurement in Education, 18*, 163-183.
